en: 'He will take me out on patrol,' I thought,
And came to settle in Talas.
Suckling at Kanykei's breast,
I became a choro to Zhakyp's
Only son, Manas.
Could I prosper if I pissed upon my oath?
Could I be a Muslim in faith?
I have become utterly accursed; let me go.
What should I remain here for?
Ill-minded Kyrgylchal,
Let me bring you down as well.
I shall keep an eye on you, Kyrgyz;
I will not listen, Kyrgylchal,
To such crooked, confusing words of yours!'
Akbaltai's Chubak
Mounted and set out on his way.
Traveling without moving by daylight,
The renowned hero crossed the passes,
Crossed many lands upon his chosen course.
His wits fled, his eyes blazed;
Changing moods, his insides boiled.
Agitated, Chubak pondered much:
Upon Zhakyp's only son Manas,
'I shall bring some calamity,' he thought.
His thoughts were torn apart;
The tears poured from Chubak's eyes:
'O noble Prophet, my faith is pure;
I have seen little loyalty from people.
Perhaps our branch has broken.
We too were one of the khans;
Things went awry, we became dependent.
Alas, such is our fortune.
The son of a renowned khan,
He torments him,
Sparing none of his bitter slander.
This swine, leader of the forty:
What a dog's deed he has done!'
Akbaltai's lion,
Grimacing, terribly ashamed,
Not dying though disgraced,
Not simply dying of his distress,
At fierce Manas the lion,
Too ashamed to thrust his spear,
Wishing to die but unable to die,
Unable to take his own life,
His heart sorely shaken,
The tears pouring from Chubak's eyes,
He drew the line of his resolve:
Chubak, son of Khan Baltai,
To your fierce father, Khan Manas,
He showed a bitter spectacle.
Giving six swift horses,
'Let him pursue blood vengeance for his father Alooke,' he thought.
To Konurbai in Beezhin,
To Kalcha, he sent a firm letter:
'Manas has lost his wits this year;
Kyrgylchal has become his intimate.
She too has gone elsewhere,
She who found the way through difficulties,
Manas's wife, Lady Kanykei.
If he is truly a warrior,
Let him plunder his valuables,' he said.
'Upon Zhakyp's only son Manas,
Let him bring great ruin,' he said.
'Let him press down upon his head,' he said.
'Konurbai, khan of Beezhin,
If he is truly a lord,
Let him scatter his four kinds of livestock;
Let him plunder his valuables.
Upon these Kyrgyz here,
Let him bring great ruin,' he said.
A brass spyglass with a screw fitting,
He grasped by its end and turned.
He clothed him in a costly coat,
He mounted him upon Kylzheerde;
Whirlwind-bottomed Enteri:
He sent Enteri away.
Against King Manas the sultan,
That Chubak was deeply offended;
He thought to fight him if he could.
The document tied into his belt—
That Chubak feared it,
Manas's oath invoking God.
Beloved Prince Chubak,
The great fierce hero, standing proud,
Raging like a lion,
Passed through Andijan;
Chubak fled toward his father.
He crossed Maseyil
And passed through broad Kashgar.
Skirting the lower mountains,
The Sarts who rode upon pack saddles,
He harassed those he encountered.
Finding no mountain to hurl himself against,
Chubak found no foe to fight;
No embers to wade through,
No shot to exchange in battle.
Without looking about him,
Chubak, son of Khan Baltai,
Sparing not his threadlike life,
A beloved house built off to the side:
His precious soul was crushed with misery.
Driven about by resentment,
Offended at your father the khan in Talas,
When he reached his goal,
When Kyrgylchal had stirred up trouble and offended him,
And Chubak had gone back among his people,
'He besieged Kashgar,' they said.
Throughout the Six Cities,
We heard word from someone:
'Chubak has become sultan,' they said.
I settled along a little stream;
Because of Kyrgylchal,
Because of that troublemaker,
Your father would not lie with me;
I was a neglected wife for two years.
I gathered lions from among females;
I gathered champion warriors from among women.
Beside your fierce father, the lion,
I settled in Talas.
Without making it a matter of shame or wounded pride,
We pursued his claims together;
We fought his enemies together.
Our beloved hair, thick as girth straps,
We bound firmly upon our heads
And went into battle together.
When your father neglected me,
When he cast me aside,
I made my towering head a banner;
I made a warrior of my woman's self.
Why should I tell the rest?
My foal, thus I became his equal.
When playing ordo,
When your father destroyed Ombu,
The ten sons of Orozoi the Sart,
Your heedless father,
When they buried him beneath a falling cliff,
When your mother bore the suffering,
Your father's Kumaik,
When he trotted across the hills,
To me, your disgraced, wretched mother,
When Kumaik came running,
Your father and the forty choros were missing.
I took Zulpukor in my hand;
All the weapons of war
I fastened tightly about my waist.
My beloved hair, thick as a girth strap,
I bound firmly upon my head.
A blue greatcoat no shot could pierce,
I put on over everything.
Your mother's black, blaze-faced argymak:
I saddled him and mounted.
Your father's Kumaik:
Following him, I set out on the road.
Following Kumaik,
I gained honor through this.
I died before my death;
When he lay beneath the cliff,
I found your father the khan.
I hurried them into a flurry;
To bring your father out alive,
To restore him to life,
The great champion who could lift a camel,
Akayar, I made him dig.
The white hunting hound saw and marked the spot,
Whining and clawing at the earth.
Your precious father, the lord,
I found him when he was dead.
I had the cliff's earth scattered;
Your father's forty mighty warriors,
Before they could say this or that,
In the blinking of an eye,
I had it opened without a moment's pause.
I kindled his extinguished fire;
I brought his dead soul to life.
I gathered what had scattered;
I did not stand watching like a mere wife.
Your campaigning father Manas,
I gave him strength when he went against the foe.
All forty were sons of forty khans;
Those forty choros, my foal,
I skillfully made into one people.
Without merely keeping house and looking on,
I made a lion of my woman's self.
Your father Manas's
Wishes I brought to fulfillment.
All his chests
I filled with yellow gold and possessions.
I built him into a house;
I planted him into an orchard.
Your leopard father Manas,
Hearing words from Kyrgylchal,
'My wife, fierce Kanykei,
Has proved dishonorable,' he heard.
'I shall search the roads of the world,' he said.
'Since my wife has turned bad,
Though I fight for many years,
Karacha's daughter Saikal
I shall take as my bride,' he said.
He took forty choros with him:
Azhybai and Khan Bakai,
Syrgak, son of Khan Ulak,
Almambet, son of Khan Azyz;
All the mighty warriors were there.
Your leopard father Manas,
Hearing word in the tales,
That among women, Khan Saikal
Had risen as a mighty warrior,
Yielding nothing to her foes,
When Konurbai, khan of Kakan,
Came pouring in to attack,
Leopard Saikal would not yield.
The beloved land of the Lop River,
She skillfully made her own domain;
The Kyrgyz and Oigut of Lop,
She skillfully made into one people.
Karacha's Saikal
Had risen as a hero, he heard.
A maiden born a leopard,
He heard she had risen as a champion.
'Since my bad wife Kanykei
Has turned out a fool,
I shall bring slaughter upon the world,' he said.
'Karacha's Khan Saikal,
Though I have to fight her,
I shall take her for my wife,' he said.
Taking ammunition loaded upon elephants,
With the learned Bakai among them,
He took a force of forty dignitaries.
He had the shotproof coats folded
And loaded upon Zhelmayan.
Their spears rang out;
He had all their guns made ready.
The leaders of ten bobbed in their saddles.
Your saintly father, that beloved lion,
Overbearingly set his course toward Maiden Saikal.
He would not hear my words though I begged;
He made me a neglected wife.
In the end, without looking upon me,
Your father Manas would not stop.
He crossed Kotormo
And passed through Suusamyr.
Traveling along Naryn,
He traveled far, sparing no horses.
Sweeping along the high plateau,
Zhaman-Echki and Taragai:
He traveled along them.
He crossed Bikirtik;
Beyond lay great Turpan.
He passed through great Turpan.
Traveling along Zhaman-Suu,
He traveled far, sparing no horses.
He forded Kum-Aryk;
Beyond lay the great plain.
He reached great Ak-Kum.
Traveling toward Lop,
